extracted.intended_audience: public relations counselors, business executives, advertisers and corporate communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for corporate public relations and propaganda: how businesses should shape public opinion, structure campaigns, and manage contacts with stakeholders to create goodwill and demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage group formation and leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilization of the group formation of modern society in order to spread ideas; leaders who lend their authority will do so only if the campaign touches their own interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use respected leaders, committees, or institutions (artists, educators, school superintendents) to lend authority; ensure the activity appeals to leaders' interests so they will endorse it. Example: nationwide Ivory soap sculpture competitions sponsored by art authorities and school systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find coincidence of interests (disinterested aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one of the functions of the public relations counsel to discover at what points his client's interests coincide with those of other individuals or groups; there must be a disinterested aspect of the propagandist's activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns so they genuinely advance interests shared with target groups (e.g., promoting aesthetic education while promoting a soap product). Avoid purely self-interested appeals that lack public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use participatory campaigns tied to respected institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Create competitions, school projects, or other participatory programs under the auspices of organizations of high standing to build prestige and mass involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure local-to-national funnels (local contests → regional → national) and engage school curricula, judges, and galleries to amplify reach and legitimacy; example: soap sculpture entries progressing to a national art gallery with distinguished judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the public: structure, personality, prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: The man in charge of a firm's public relations must be familiar with the structure, the prejudices, and the whims of the general public, and must handle his problems with the utmost care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research audience norms and limits; tailor messaging so it conforms to public standards and tastes rather than attempting to dictate radical changes directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous interpretation vs. dramatization (highspotting)
rubrics_metrics.description: General plan of work reduced to two types: continuous interpretation (control every approach so impressions form unconsciously) and dramatization by high-spotting (vividly seize attention on a typical detail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose method(s) after studying objectives and possibilities; both can be used concurrently. Example of highspotting: making a building deliberately taller to dramatize prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage every public touchpoint to dramatize personality
rubrics_metrics.description: A business must dramatize its personality and interpret its objectives in every particular in which it comes into contact with the community (architecture, delivery wagons, doorman, cleanliness, employee compensation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistency across physical appearance, customer service, facilities, and corporate leaders' public behavior because trivial details influence public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and truthful interpretation (avoid deceptive protective coloring)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations activities of a business cannot be a protective coloring to hide its real aims; a sound public relations policy will not attempt to stampede the public with exaggerated claims and false pretenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misrepresentative displays (e.g., showcasing a few high-class items when main stock is cheap). Use truthful, vivid interpretation rather than deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target intermediaries and institutional adopters when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns may be directed not to the public but to other elements (railroads, steamship companies, foreign governments) whose cooperation will advantage the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and persuade intermediaries or institutions whose policy changes will indirectly increase product use or sales (e.g., get hospitals/schools to use a product as a demonstration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create services/institutions that serve public good and product interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop bureaus, information services, or institutions (investment services, insurance departments, foot protection bureaus) that both help the public and promote the product's virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design genuinely useful services tied to the product's features so civic bodies and opinion leaders will support and disseminate the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use credible research and pilot adoption to build momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove advantages by research (Mellon Institute gelatine tests) and have hospitals/schools test the product; project favorable results to leaders who then adopt and influence others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage scientific institutions and early adopter leaders to create credibility and diffusion of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and respond to trends in public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations counsel should anticipate trends and advise how to avert unfavorable shifts either by persuasion or by modifying client action; survey public opinion to discover irreducible opposition and points susceptible to explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct public opinion research, identify emotional vs. logical factors, and recommend policy or communication changes accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfill responsibilities to multiple stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Businesses have responsibilities to stockholders, dealers, industry, retailers, consumers and the general public; each of these relationships must be managed (e.g., furnish information to stockholders, invite dealers to factories, maintain hygienic production for consumers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor communication and programs to each stakeholder group; neglect of any stakeholder can damage overall public relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt product/policy and even trivial details to public demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended modifications may concern the broadest matters of policy or the most trivial details of execution (product lines, clerk dress, branch location) to make the business conform to public objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to recommend substantive changes (product mix, branches) or small executional changes (employee behavior, store appearance) to align with public expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PR to combat unethical or exaggerated advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations can break down unfair competitive exaggerated advertising by reaching the public with the truth through non-advertising channels (dental clinics, schools, medical colleges, women's clubs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate credible channels (professional institutions, press, clubs) to present factual counter-information rather than engaging in reciprocal exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate industry-level responses to inter-commodity competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-commodity and inter-industrial competition often requires cooperative propaganda by trade associations; individual firms cannot always fight alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize associations or cooperative campaigns to address competition between different product categories that vie for the same consumer dollar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain ongoing engagement to support mass-production demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass production requires constant touch with the public through advertising and propaganda to assure continuous demand; making customers is the new problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement continuous communication strategies to sustain demand rather than sporadic advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid running counter to public norms; work through leaders to change taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The public is not an amorphous mass; you may not persuade a whole generation directly but can work via leaders (fashion leaders) to effect gradual change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use opinion leaders and gradual, targeted influence rather than attempting abrupt mass changes that contradict entrenched public habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acceptance and transparency are vital for financing and mergers
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of stock or bond flotations and mergers depends upon the general record of the concern and the goodwill it has created; public acceptance can create real economic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a track record of transparency and goodwill; avoid reliance on dishonest propaganda or manipulation, instead foster genuine public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small details and leaders' personal reputations affect corporate goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: Trivial things (employee housing, charity contributions, president's scandals) can influence public opinion; the personality of corporate leaders may dramatize the whole concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and manage leaders' public behavior and seemingly minor corporate details because they have outsized effects on public perception.
